power_for_place.why: A has the more consistent tier progression: early seeds, middle-tier enablers, then meaningful multipliers and capstones. B puts substantial repeatable scaling on cheap cards, while some later pieces offer comparatively little. Estimates below use normal copies and plausible setups; transferred stats are not automatically new board stats.

A_outliers.issue: Three to five Challenges add 9–15 combat damage, versus the T3 in-fight median of 4.5. That is unusually efficient support for an already useful extra-attack mechanic.
Two or three Chieftain deaths distribute 12–18 combat stats, versus the T3 median of 4.5. The crown automatically finding another recipient makes this condition fairly dependable.

B_outliers.issue: Two or three adjacent sales produce 6–9 permanent stats per turn, versus the T1 median of 2. Sales cost resources, but ordinary cycling already exceeds the tier's scaling budget substantially.
With four other Ogres, three adjacent sales add 12 permanent stats, versus the T3 median of 5.5. This becomes the wide engine's scaling backbone unusually early.

Usually adds roughly 0–4 permanent stats per fight, versus the T4 median of 12 per turn. Target selection is valuable, but a 5/6 without an extra attack struggles to kill the highest-Attack enemy and earn even that modest payoff.

Ordinary purchased fodder supplies approximately 7–12 permanent stats once per turn, around half the T5 median of 20. Selling an already-buffed ally mostly consolidates existing stats. External Tavern buffs can rescue it, but its native scaling is weak for T5.

power_for_place.A_tier_jobs: T1–2 establish feeding, economy and Challenge access. T3 clearly names the compositions, although Clubsmith and Cho'Rush overdeliver. T4 supplies substantial scaling and useful support; Kingmaker's zero net stats have a credible redistribution purpose. T5 adds succession, combat chaining and buff duplication. Gruul, Cho'gall and Mar'gok provide recognizable T6 payoffs.
power_for_place.B_tier_jobs: T1–2 establish fodder and selling rewards effectively. T3 already contains much of the main engine's scaling. T4 is mixed: Mound-Matron's three 3/3 summons supply 18 combat stats, close to the 20 median, while Challenger lags. T5 offers interesting modifiers but uneven independent value. T6 Gordok transforms the engine; Mar'gok supplies at most 36 permanent stats per turn, respectable but below the 53 median.

distinctiveness.why: A more thoroughly changes interaction between opposing boards: players deliberately attack the enemy carry, build decoys, and manage crown succession across recruitment and combat. B's empty-space commitment is genuinely bold, but its central buy–sell–multiply engine is closer to familiar transaction-based play. King Gordok also removes the adjacency decision that initially distinguishes Tribute.
distinctiveness.A_core: Challenge combines deliberate opening attacks with a transferable, type-independent Chieftain. Enforcer, Kingmaker and King Gordok make targeting and leadership manipulable resources. Two-Headed adds a smaller timing layer.
distinctiveness.B_core: Tribute makes sale order and adjacency productive; empty-space rewards turn board size into a resource. Bickering Ogre Magi makes the side of a sale matter, while Hermit, Ko'ragh and Mar'gok support deliberately keeping fewer bodies.

A_has_B_lost: Enforcer lets another tribe's Venomous, Divine Shield or Rally minion become a targeted opening attacker; B's Challenger keeps targeting to itself and grants no opening attack. Kingmaker and King Gordok also create a concrete succession game that B's king lacks.
B_has_A_lost: B makes vacancies valuable: Hermit and Mar'gok reward keeping gaps, Ringmaster compensates for fewer attackers, and Ko'ragh converts gaps into Divine Shields. Bickering Ogre Magi also gives left-versus-right placement an immediate economic consequence. A has no comparable reason to keep a smaller board.
